 More parents are declining vitamin K shots for newborns, putting more babies at risk of bleeding: Study 
 With shot numbers declining, a study found more babies are at risk of bleeding. 
 By Dr. Jade Cobern and Mary Kekatos November 5, 2026, 11:05 AM 
 4:25 Adobe Stock For most of his nearly 30-year career, Dr. Thomas Patterson rarely had a parent refuse the vitamin K shot   for their newborn, which is recommended at birth to protect babies from severe bleeding   in   early   life.  
 However, what Patterson says was once uncommon has become a regular occurrence when the Idaho pediatrician is working in a   newborn nursery in the southwest region of the state.
 "Prior to, say [20]22 or so, vitamin K refusals were very sporadic and rare, and they weren't all-consuming," Patterson told ABC News. "There has been a significant uptick for me ... One day [this year], I had 10 babies and five of them went out of the hospital without vitamin K."  
 Adobe Stock What Patterson is seeing is reflected in new research published in JAMA on Thursday from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP).  
 Speaking first to ABC News, two of the study's authors said these findings built upon previous research the team had done. The new study   included updated data from 2025, which showed an increasing number of babies who are not receiving vitamin K injections at birth.  
 "This is certainly evidence that more babies are not receiving vitamin K, and more babies are at risk of bleeding," Dr. Kristan Scott, lead author of the study, former research fellow at CHOP, and now an assistant professor of pediatrics at Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, told ABC News.
 After analyzing more than 5.2   million health records from Epic Cosmos data, the team said they   found that from 2017 to 2025,   the percentage   of babies who didn't receive a vitamin K shot at birth more than doubled   from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025.  
 Percentage of babies who did not receive the vitamin K shot at birth, 2017-2025 JAMA, Epic Cosmos Related More parents are refusing vitamin K shots for newborns, doctors say. Here's why that could be dangerous Between 2024 and 2025, the percentage of babies who did not receive the vitamin K shot rose by about   20%, from 5.6% to 6.8%, respectively, in the   study.
 "It's certainly not something that I wanted to see but I think, given the trend in what we had seen from years prior, it was not [surprising]," Scott said.  
 Why the vitamin K shot is given to newborns   
 Vitamin K is necessary to help the body form clots appropriately, but babies are born with   very small   amounts of this vitamin and don't receive adequate amounts through their diet in the first few months of life.
 This   puts   them at increased risk of a condition called vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB), according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention   (CDC).
 STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images To help prevent   this   bleeding, a vitamin K injection has been recommended for newborns in the U.S. since the early 1960s .   It's   given as a single, intramuscular shot soon after birth.
 "Vitamin K is absolutely critical for our livers to make the clotting factors that help our blood clot," Dr. David Hill, a hospitalist, pediatrician and spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), told ABC News. "What we're really worried about is serious life-threatening bleeding ... And often, by the time we figure out that bleeding is happening, it's really too late to stop the worst consequences of it."
 Since this injection became standard of care, doctors say it   is very rare   for babies to experience   VKDB in the U.S., but they worry more babies will suffer from bleeding complications as more parents refuse the shot.
 Related 5 things for parents to know about changes to kids' vaccine schedule In Hill's experience, Vitamin K refusal   "has increased dramatically, and we're talking about an intervention that we have been using safely and effectively since 1961."
 Possible li f elong complications   
 Newborns who do not receive the vitamin K shot at birth are at a higher risk of life-threatening bleeding.
 Of the infants who have late VKDB --   between 2   weeks old and 6 months old --- about half have brain bleeds, which can lead to permanent brain damage, according to the CDC .  
 Other infants bleed into their stomachs or intestines, or other parts of the body. Many of these infants will require blood transfusions, and some may need surgeries, the CDC says.  
 Related Changes to hepatitis B vaccine recommendations could leave millions of children vulnerable: Study There are often no warning signs of VKDB, according to the agency.  
 In the new study, researchers also analyzed   bleeding events documented in medical records at certain timepoints after birth through the first six months of life, among babies born at 35 to 43 weeks' gestation.

 They found that from 2017 to 2025, the rate of bleeding events increased among all babies, but more so among those who did not receive vitamin K at birth.
 Bleeding events in infants who received vitamin K shot vs. those who did not, 2017-2025 JAMA, Epic Cosmos These babies had a 47% increased risk of any bleeding event in their first six months of life, compared to those who did receive a vitamin K shot at birth,   according to the study's findings.
 The risk of having any type of brain bleeding in the first six months of life more than doubled without the shot, and the risk of death during the birth hospitalization also more than doubled among babies who didn't receive a shot of vitamin K at birth, the study found.  
 "When you don't get vitamin K today, we see very similar rates to what bleeding rates were before the routine administration of vitamin K," Dr. Heather Burris, a study author, neonatologist at CHOP and professor of pediatrics at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania,   told ABC News.
 A syringe is shown in this undated file photo. STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images Dr. Scott Hadland, a pediatrician   at Mass General Brigham for Children, said he cares for many older children, adolescents and young adults who have long-term complications from severe brain bleeding.
 "I've cared for a few patients who had a severe bleed shortly after birth, and it was likely caused by lack of vitamin K," he said.  
 In general, Hadland said   some patients with severe brain bleeds in infancy can develop long-term movement problems, including cerebral palsy, may   develop behavioral challenges, or   may require a shunt to manage high pressures around their brain.
 "A lot of families are thinking about their baby in the moment but not realizing that the decision they make [not to get the vitamin K shot] actually has consequences that can last for decades," he added.
 Related As measles continues to spread, health officials are seeing vaccine interest rise Death is also a risk. Twenty percent of babies with VKDB -- one out of every five -- die, according to the CDC .  
 Patterson, the pediatrician from Idaho, said he's heard from colleagues across the state who have treated babies in the neonatal intensive care unit   with brain bleeds after not getting the vitamin K shot.  
 "We can't put a number on the exact number of deaths, but I know of at least two. I could easily say three with some confidence," Patterson said. "As someone who's done first responder resuscitations for babies for decades, I   have videos in my head of every baby that's ever lost their life on my watch. I have been fortunate not to see that because ...   of refusal of vitamin K."  
 Why is this happening?   
 Doctors told ABC News there are several reasons that some parents have refused the vitamin K shot for their newborns.  
 Patterson said many parents bring up that vitamin K has a black box warning. It's most stringent the FDA can require from a drug manufacturer, requiring that clinical data shows the drug can cause severe harm, hospitalization or death.
 However, the warning is based on a risk that applies to adults who are receiving high, intravenous doses -- not the much smaller, intramuscular vitamin K dose babies receive.  
 Some parents have also refused the vitamin K shot as a larger rejection of examination because parents worry it "creates trauma,"   Patterson, from Idaho, said.  
 STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images Doctors told ABC News some of the refusals have   been   fueled by misinformation, such as fears that   the preservative in the shot could harm children, which there is no scientific evidence of, while others have confused the vitamin injection with a vaccine.
 "I have families who think maybe this is a vaccine, but it's very important to emphasize this is a naturally occurring vitamin that we all have and that we all need," said Hill, the AAP spokesperson. "It has nothing to do with vaccines."  
 Doctors suggested that parents speak to a trusted healthcare provider or their pediatrician before refusing the vitamin K shot.  
 Related Doctors push back on Trump executive order to change childhood vaccine schedule To explain its protective effects, Burris, from CHOP, likened receiving the shot to wearing a seatbelt in a car.  
 "The chances of having a serious bleed and having a consequence of that bleeding is going to go way down if you get the vitamin K shot, just like if you get in a car crash and you're wearing your seatbelt, you are less likely to sustain serious injuries," she said.  
 "So, I think it's really important for us to think about vitamin K as a preventative measure that we can do. It's a simple pinprick of a shot."  
 Jade A. Cobern, MD, MPH, is a practicing physician, board-certi f ied in pediatrics and general preventive medicine, and is a f ellow o f the ABC News Medical Unit.
